extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate/Putnam contestants and problem-solvers; problem-committee members
extracted.subtask_description: A collection of Putnam-style contest problems (proposed by R. Stanley for the 1984–86 Putnam Exams). Tasks require producing rigorous solutions, constructions, or counterexamples and often require answers in a specified canonical form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difficulty labeling (A1 or B1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Problems intended to be A1 or B1 (and therefore relatively easy) are marked accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the A1/B1 marks to set expectations for relative difficulty and expected length/complexity of a solution. A1/B1 problems are intended to be relatively easy compared with other Putnam problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof / rigorous justification requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: When a problem states 'Find (with proof)' or 'Prove or disprove', the solver must provide a rigorous proof of the asserted statement or a valid counterexample together with justification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most problems explicitly require proofs or disproofs; answers consisting of unproven assertions, heuristic arguments, or numerical experiments without proof are not acceptable. Provide clear logical steps, and when asked to show minimality, maximality, existence, or uniqueness, justify those properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Answer-format conformity (express in specified canonical form)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a problem asks to 'Express' or 'Find' the answer in a specific form (for example, 'in the form a! b! c! d! / n!', 'Find a rational number r', 'Express S in the form (π^2/6) k', or 'Find a formula of the form a1 b1^n + a2 b2^n + ...'), the final answer must be presented in that requested canonical form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the exact formatting/representation requested by the problem. Examples from the text: problem 8 asks the triple integral value 'in the form a! b! c! d! / n!'; problem 21 requests expressing S in the form (π^2/6)·k; problem 10 asks for f(n) in a sum of exponentials a_i b_i^n. If intermediate simplification is used, show steps that lead to the canonical representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction vs. existence requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: When a problem asks for a set, polynomial, matrix, integers, or other object 'Find ...' or 'Find with proof a set ... for which this minimum k is achieved,' the solver must either explicitly construct an example meeting the stated property or prove that none exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For existence statements require explicit construction or demonstration; for optimality/minimality also prove that no better example exists. For 'show that no such P(x) exists' style prompts, provide a proof of impossibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conventions and representation choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Problems sometimes fix conventions or representation choices that must be adhered to (examples: 'By convention, the sum of the elements of the empty set is 0.'; for binary expansions 'say we never choose the expansion ending in infinitely many 1’s').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adhere to stated conventions when interpreting or manipulating objects. For instance, use the empty-sum = 0 rule in combinatorial sums; for binary expansions choose the non-terminating-ones representation as specified to make definitions (like reading binary as ternary) unambiguous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combinatorial/counting closed-form requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: When a problem asks for the number of objects or for a formula (e.g., 'Find, as a function of n, max over full subsets S ... expressed as a polynomial in n' or 'Find a formula for f(n) of the form ...'), the expected solution is a closed-form expression (polynomial, explicit formula, or finite combination of standard functions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derive an exact formula rather than just asymptotics or bounds; when requested, express the answer as a polynomial, rational function, or specified finite sum of exponentials as directed. Provide proof that the formula holds for all required n and any deduced domain constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extremal/optimization and existence-of-maximum caution
rubrics_metrics.description: When a problem asks to find the maximum or show 'no maximum exists' (e.g., 'Find the maximum value, or show that no maximum exists'), the solver must either produce the maximizing configuration and prove optimality, or prove rigorously that no maximum exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include arguments establishing attainment (compactness/continuity/constructive bound) or demonstrate sequences exhibiting unbounded behavior or approach to supremum without attainment, as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modular/periodicity and dependence-only-on-sum statements
rubrics_metrics.description: For problems asserting that some function depends only on a sum or is periodic (e.g., problem 9: last nonzero digit f(5a1+...+5ak) depends only on sum, and there may be a period p with g(s)=g(s+p)), the solver must prove dependence/periodicity statements and either exhibit the period or prove nonexistence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide number-theoretic or combinatorial proofs showing invariance under permutations or reduction mod appropriate values; if claiming a period, give a proof and compute the least period or show impossibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power-series/radius-of-convergence and analytic-form requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: When a problem defines power series and asks for radius of convergence or analytic properties in terms of parameters (e.g., 'Find the largest real number R for which the power series F(u)=Σ f(n,n,n) u^n converges for all |u|<R'), solutions must compute or bound convergence radii and justify analyticity regions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use standard tests (ratio/root, comparison) and any combinatorial estimates for coefficients f(n,n,n) to produce rigorous bounds for the radius of convergence; explicitly justify steps leading to the largest admissible R.
